A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same adaptive KV-cache budget-allocation work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, proofs, and appendices are readable and matchable despite retitling and reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations on 16 LongBench datasets using Mistral and LWM, Needle-in-a-Haystack results, and attention-concentration and eviction-bound analyses.

after.justification: V3 retains the LongBench experiments, updates Needle-in-a-Haystack results, and reports additional measured eviction-loss, memory, and decoding-latency results.

M1.justification: The global Top-k allocator and alpha safeguard are retained. V3's Algorithm 3 explicitly reserves the observation-window budget and retains window tokens, whereas v1's abbreviated procedure lacks these steps. The PDFs do not resolve whether this changes underlying eviction behavior or documents existing implementation more fully.

E1.justification: The same 16 LongBench datasets, task types, and languages remain. Needle-in-a-Haystack coverage extends beyond v1's 217K maximum to 429K for SnapKV/Ada-SnapKV and 365K for Pyramid/Ada-Pyramid, adding longer-input conditions within the existing retrieval task.

E2.justification: Corresponding LongBench comparisons retain Full Cache, H2O, StreamingLLM, SnapKV, and Pyramid; Needle-in-a-Haystack quality comparisons retain SnapKV and Pyramid against their adaptive versions. The new efficiency analyses use existing comparators, and newly cited methods are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V3 introduces normalized output-L1-loss evaluation on 200 Qasper samples at 5% and 10% cache retention, plus peak-memory and decoding-latency measurements across context lengths. Section 4.3 changes the Needle-in-a-Haystack context grid and reports a full-cache limit of 37K instead of 33K. LongBench models, metrics, and budget settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V1's Figure 3 plots layerwise upper bounds for one Qasper example; v3 replaces this with actual relative eviction losses across 200 examples at two retention ratios in Figure 4. Appendix A.2 adds resource-scaling analyses testing the efficiency of adaptive allocation. The existing head-concentration analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V3's variation across individual Qasper samples is additional empirical evidence, not uncertainty estimation or repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: Both LongBench result tables are numerically unchanged. Under revised context coverage, Needle-in-a-Haystack scores change from 95.40/96.56 to 94.84/95.99 for SnapKV/Ada-SnapKV, and from 96.62/97.02 to 96.02/96.69 for Pyramid/Ada-Pyramid. These are replaced results under different conditions, not same-setting performance declines. V3 also adds actual-loss and memory/latency findings.

T1.justification: The four theorems and their central arguments remain. V3 corrects the appendix definition of C from the matrix 1-norm in v1's Appendix A.2 to the infinity/max-row norm in Appendix A.4, aligning it with the main theorem and proof. Section 3.2 also explicitly states the one-token observation-window assumption.

C1.justification: V3 makes empirical L1 eviction-loss reduction and efficient CUDA implementation explicit main contributions. V1's abstract and contribution list principally emphasized upper-bound optimization and generation quality. The central adaptive-allocation claim and the Ada-SnapKV/Ada-Pyramid contributions remain.

C2.justification: V3 distinguishes Theorem 4's upper-bound guarantee from empirical actual-loss reduction, replacing v1's inference that the theorem itself ensures smaller actual loss. It explains critical-cache stability and the alpha safeguard more explicitly, and adds discussion of combining eviction with quantization and query-aware cache recall.

D1.justification: V1's Appendix A.7 promises future code release; v3's abstract reports code availability. V3 additionally documents flattened cache storage with a custom CUDA kernel, 16-bit inference, a single A100-80G for all experiments, post-prefill eviction, and explicit observation-window accounting. These substantially expand implementation and reproducibility information without establishing when the implementation changed.

R1.justification: V3 adds references including Longformer, LM-Infinite, Scissorhands, Ren and Zhu, and attention-head specialization studies. Section 2 introduces a sliding-window versus Top-k taxonomy, while Appendix A.1 expands discussion of complementary techniques. The fundamental positioning of adaptive allocation relative to existing eviction methods remains.

P1.justification: The title introduces Ada-KV, and the abstract, introduction, related work, and method narrative are extensively rewritten. The six-subsection Framework becomes a four-subsection Method section, combining theoretical and empirical allocation discussions. Appendix sections are reordered and references move after the appendix text.

P2.justification: V3 adds the eviction overview, redraws the allocation example, replaces the bound plot with measured-loss plots, adds memory/latency figures, and reformats the retrieval heatmaps. Retained displays are relocated or rescaled, and the proof appendix changes to two columns. The redrawn Figure 2 introduces a caption mismatch: it shows six elements per head while saying five.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens evidence for the proposal's practical value. V1's one-example upper-bound plot did not directly establish smaller actual attention-output error; v3 tests that error on 200 samples and adds memory/decoding-cost comparisons addressing efficient execution. Clearer assumptions, the norm correction, and expanded implementation information improve assessability and reproducibility. The new Figure 2 caption mismatch is a limited presentation defect outweighed by these gains; the unchanged LongBench tables and altered retrieval settings do not establish a same-setting accuracy improvement.
